props.title: Carlos

sections.content: Carlos (2010) stands as one of cinema's most ambitious portraits of international terrorism, with Édgar Ramírez delivering a tour-de-force performance as Ilich Ramírez Sánchez, aka Carlos the Jackal. Director Olivier Assayas crafts a sprawling 5.5-hour epic that revolutionized how political thrillers handle complex historical material. Like Munich (2005) and The Baader Meinhof Complex (2008), it captures the volatile atmosphere of 1970s political violence, but with unprecedented scope and granular detail.

sections.content: What sets Carlos apart is its unflinching examination of how ideology morphs into ego-driven violence. The film shares DNA with Che (2008) in its epic scope and political complexity, but Assayas takes a colder, more clinical approach. We watch Carlos transform from a committed revolutionary into a gun-for-hire, parallel to how The Battle of Algiers (1966) shows the evolution of urban warfare tactics.

The film's technical achievements are staggering. Assayas shoots across multiple continents, recreating famous incidents like the 1975 OPEC raid with documentary-like precision. The attention to period detail rivals Good Bye, Lenin! (2003) and The Lives of Others (2006), while the narrative complexity echoes Syriana (2005) in its web of international intrigue. sections.content: Carlos marked a crucial shift in how cinema depicts political violence. Unlike the straightforward heroics of Munich (2005) or the psychological focus of United 93 (2006), Assayas presents terrorism as a complex network of competing interests - personal, political, and financial. This approach influenced later works like Zero Dark Thirty (2012) and A Most Wanted Man (2014).
